statements: The chief complaint is chronic left hip pain for 1 year.
The left hip pain is worsened by exercise.
The left hip pain is especially worsened by hip flexion.
The left hip pain has intensified over the past 1 week.
The patient has constitutional symptoms over 2 months.
The patient has malaise.
The patient has anorexia.
The patient has lost 6 kg in 1 month.
The constitutional symptoms raise concern for a neoplastic rather than purely mechanical musculoskeletal process.
Pain is reproduced when the left hip is flexed beyond 40 degrees.
Pain is reproduced particularly when the left hip is flexed against resistance.
The pain localization suggests pathology in the iliopsoas or hip flexor region.
The patient has numbness in the left lower extremity provoked by hip flexion.
The hip-flexion-provoked numbness suggests local mass effect on adjacent neural structures.
The FABER test is positive.
Imaging shows a discrete soft-tissue mass.
CT demonstrated a 64×29-mm noninvasive mass posterior to the psoas muscle.
The CT mass contains amorphous calcifications.
MRI showed a 72×45×50-mm lobulated mass arising from the left iliopsoas muscle.
The MRI mass is sharply marginated.
The MRI mass extends along fat planes.
The MRI mass is T1 hypointense in calcified areas.
The MRI mass is T2 hyperintense.
The MRI mass shows marked postcontrast enhancement.
These imaging features strongly support a calcified soft-tissue neoplasm centered in muscle.
The patient denied trauma.
The absence of trauma argues against post-traumatic myositis ossificans or hematoma.
CBC was normal.
ESR was normal.
CRP was normal.
Electrolytes were normal.
Liver tests were normal.
Renal tests were normal.
The normal laboratory tests make infection such as psoas abscess unlikely.
The normal laboratory tests do not support an inflammatory arthropathy.
Pelvic radiograph showed no acute osseous abnormality.
The normal pelvic radiograph argues against a primary bony lesion extending secondarily.
There was no motor weakness.
The gait was normal.
The absence of motor weakness and the normal gait suggest localized rather than advanced neurologic compromise.
The leading differential is extraskeletal osteosarcoma of the iliopsoas.
Extraskeletal osteosarcoma fits a painful deep soft-tissue mass with calcifications or ossification.
Extraskeletal osteosarcoma fits marked enhancement and constitutional symptoms.
Extraskeletal osteosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor producing osteoid in soft tissue without attachment to bone.
The imaging description of an intramuscular calcified mass with no osseous involvement is highly compatible with extraskeletal osteosarcoma.
A second consideration is myositis ossificans.
Myositis ossificans can present as a calcified intramuscular mass.
Myositis ossificans can present with pain on motion.
Myositis ossificans is less likely because there is no trauma history.
Myositis ossificans is less likely because the course is prolonged with systemic symptoms and weight loss.
Myositis ossificans is less likely because the lesion is described as a lobulated enhancing mass rather than the more typical zonal peripheral ossification pattern.
Another differential is synovial sarcoma or another soft-tissue sarcoma with calcification.
Synovial sarcoma can occur near joints in younger to middle-aged adults.
Synovial sarcoma may calcify.
Synovial sarcoma can be painful.
The lesion is specifically arising from the iliopsoas muscle.
The lesion contains amorphous calcifications suggestive of osteoid matrix.
These findings make extraskeletal osteosarcoma a better fit than synovial sarcoma.
Tumoral calcinosis is less likely.
Tumoral calcinosis can present as calcified periarticular masses.
Tumoral calcinosis is usually composed of lobulated calcific deposits without this pattern of enhancing intramuscular soft-tissue tumor.
Tumoral calcinosis is not typically associated with weight loss or progressive pain from hip flexion.
Calcific myonecrosis is also unlikely.
Calcific myonecrosis is unlikely given the absence of remote trauma history.
Calcific myonecrosis is unlikely given the absence of compartment syndrome history.

The combination of chronic progressive hip pain localized to the iliopsoas, constitutional symptoms, a sharply marginated enhancing intramuscular mass with amorphous calcifications, and no bone involvement most strongly supports extraskeletal osteosarcoma arising in the left iliopsoas muscle.
Extraskeletal osteosarcoma of the left iliopsoas muscle is the high-probability differential diagnosis.
Myositis ossificans is a medium-probability differential diagnosis.
Synovial sarcoma is a medium-probability differential diagnosis.
Psoas abscess is a low-probability differential diagnosis.
Hip pain with psoas involvement is possible in psoas abscess.
Normal CBC, ESR, and CRP make psoas abscess unlikely.
The absence of fever makes psoas abscess unlikely.
A calcified enhancing mass makes psoas abscess unlikely.
The final diagnosis is extraskeletal osteosarcoma of the left iliopsoas muscle.
